cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XII
The Sirens;\nScylla and Charybdis; the cattle of the Sun.
Now when the ship had left the stream of the river\nOcean and come out into the swell of the wide-wayed sea
and the island of Aeaea — where the house of early-born
Dawn is, and her dancing-grounds, and the risings\nof the sun — we ran her in there onto the sands
and stepped out ourselves onto the surf-line of the sea,
and there we dropped asleep, and waited for shining Dawn.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nthen I sent companions ahead to the house of Circe
to bring the body of Elpenor, who had died.
We cut billets of wood, quickly,\nand where the headland ran out highest
we buried him, grieving, letting the big tears fall.
And when the dead man was burned,\nand the dead man's armor,
we heaped a mound, and dragged a pillar-stone onto it,
and on the very top of the mound\nwe fixed his well-shaped oar.
So we saw to it all, each thing.\nAnd our coming up from Hades
was not lost on Circe: she readied herself and\ncame quickly, and her handmaids with her carried
bread and meat in plenty and fire-bright red wine.
And she stood in our midst and spoke,\nshining among goddesses:
'Hard men — you who went down\nliving into the house of Hades:
twice-dying, when other men die once.
Come now: eat your food, and drink your wine,\nhere, all day long. And when dawn shows
you shall sail; and I will point out your road,\nand make each thing plain, so that no grinding evil design,
on sea or on land, can catch you and make you suffer.'
So she spoke, and our proud hearts consented.
So then all day long till the setting of the sun we\nsat feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine;
and when the sun went down and the dusk came on,\nthe men lay down to sleep beside the ship's stern-cables,
but she took me by the hand,\napart from my dear companions,
and made me sit, and lay beside me,\nand asked me everything;
and I told it all through to her, in its due order.
And then the lady Circe spoke to me in words:
'So all that has been brought to its end. Now hear
what I will tell you — and a god\nhimself will bring it back to your mind.
First you will come to the Sirens,\nwho enchant all mankind — whoever comes upon them.
Whoever in ignorance draws near and hears the\nvoice of the Sirens — no wife, no little children
will ever stand beside that man to welcome him home;
no — the Sirens enchant him with their clear-toned song,
sitting in a meadow; and around\nthem is a great heap of the bones
of rotting men, and the skins are shriveling on them.
Drive past them; and knead honey-sweet wax
and stop your companions' ears with it,\nso that none of the others
may hear. But you yourself — listen, if you will:
only let them bind you in the fast ship, hand and foot,
upright in the mast-step, with the\nrope-ends made fast to the mast itself,
so that you may hear the two\nSirens' voice, and delight in it.
And if you beg your companions —\nif you order them to free you —
then let them bind you down with still more bonds.
But when your companions have driven past them,\nfrom there I will not spell it out for you to the end —
which of two roads will be yours. You yourself must\nweigh it in your heart. But I will tell you both.
On the one side, overhanging rocks; and against\nthem roars the great swell of dark-eyed Amphitrite.
The blessed gods call them the Wandering Rocks.
That way not even winged things pass — not even\nthe shy doves that carry ambrosia to father Zeus:
the sheer rock always takes one even of those,\nand the Father sends in another to keep the number full.
That way no ship of men has ever yet escaped,\nwhichever came, but ships' planks and men's bodies together
are carried off by the waves of the\nsea and the squalls of deadly fire.
One seagoing ship alone has sailed past there —\nArgo, whom all minds know — sailing home from Aeetes;
and even her the wave would have\nflung swiftly on the great rocks,
but Hera sent her through, because Jason was dear to her.
On the other side are two crags:\none reaches the wide heaven
with its sharp peak, and a dark-blue cloud rings it,\nnever drawing off — no clear sky ever holds
that summit, not in summer, not in harvest-time.
No mortal man could climb it, or set foot on the top,\nnot if he had twenty hands and twenty feet:
the rock is smooth — as if dressed smooth all around.
And in the middle of the crag is a misty cave turned\ntoward the dark, toward Erebus — the very way you
will steer your hollow ship, shining Odysseus.
Not even a strong man's arrow, shot from a hollow ship,\ncould reach up into that vaulted cave.
And in it lives Scylla — yelping horribly.
Her voice, truly, is no more than a newborn puppy's,\nbut she herself is an evil monster: no one
could look at her and rejoice —\nnot a god, if a god should meet her.
Twelve feet she has, all of them dangling;\nsix necks, immensely long, and on each one
a hideous head, and in each three rows of teeth,\nthick-set and crowded, full of black death.
Waist-deep she is sunk in the hollow of the cave,\nbut she holds her heads out of that terrible pit
and fishes there, quivering with hunger around the crag,\nfor dolphins and dogfish, and whatever bigger beast
she can seize, of the thousands\ndeep-moaning Amphitrite pastures.
Past her no sailors yet can boast to have\nfled unharmed with their ship: with each head
she carries off a man, snatched\nfrom the dark-blue-prowed vessel.
The other crag is lower — you will see it, Odysseus —\nclose by the first: a bowshot would carry across.
On it stands a great fig tree, dense in leaf,\nand beneath it shining Charybdis gulps down the black water.
Three times a day she spouts it forth,\nthree times she gulps it down —
terribly. May you not chance to be there when she gulps:
no one could save you from that evil\nthen — not the earth-shaker himself.
No: keep close to Scylla's crag,\nand quickly drive the ship past. It is far better
to mourn six companions from your ship than all together.'
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
'Come then, goddess — tell me this, and tell it true:
might I somehow slip out from under deadly Charybdis
and stand off the other,\nwhen she strikes at my companions?'
So I spoke, and she answered at once,\nshining among goddesses:
'Hard man! So even now your\nheart is set on the works of war
and struggle. Will you not yield\neven to the deathless gods?
She is not mortal — she is an immortal evil,\nterrible, grim, savage, not to be fought.
There is no defense. To flee her is the best courage.
For if you linger by the rock to arm yourself,\nI fear she will dart out a second time and catch you
with all six heads, and take six men again.
No — row past with all your force, and call on Crataiis,
the mother of Scylla, who bore her, a plague on mortals:
she will stop her then from darting out again.
And you will come to the island Thrinacia. There in plenty
graze the cattle of Helios, and his strong flocks:
seven herds of cattle, and as many fine flocks of\nsheep, fifty in each. No young are born to them,
and they never die away. Goddesses are their shepherds,\nnymphs of the lovely braids, Phaethusa and Lampetie,
whom shining Neaera bore to Helios Hyperion.
Their honored mother, when she had borne and reared them,\nsettled them far away, on the island Thrinacia,
to keep their father's sheep and his crook-horned cattle.
If you leave these unharmed,\nand keep your mind on homecoming,
then you may yet reach Ithaca, though you suffer evils;\nbut if you harm them, then I foretell destruction
for ship and companions. And even if you yourself escape,
late you will come, and in evil case,\nall companions lost.'
So she spoke; and at once Dawn\nof the golden throne came on.
Then she went away up the island, shining among goddesses,\nand I went to the ship and roused my companions
to board in their turn and loose the stern-cables;
and they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks,
and sitting in order they struck\nthe gray salt water with their oars.
And for us, behind the dark-blue-prowed ship,\na following wind that filled the sail, a good companion,
was sent by Circe of the lovely braids,\ndread goddess with a mortal's voice.
So when we had seen to the tackle through the ship,
we sat, and the wind and the steersman held her on course.
Then, grieving at heart, I spoke among my companions:
'Friends — it is not right that one man only, or two,
should know the decrees that Circe\ntold me, shining among goddesses.
No: I will speak, so that knowing them we may die —\nor swerve aside, and escape death and doom.
First she commands us to shun the marvelous Sirens —\ntheir voice, and their flowering meadow.
Me alone she bade listen to their song. But bind me
in a bond that bites, so that I stay fixed where I stand,
upright in the mast-step, with the\nrope-ends made fast to the mast itself.
And if I beg you — if I order you to free me —\nthen squeeze me down with still more bonds.'
So I went through it all, telling my companions,\nwhile the well-made ship ran swiftly on
toward the island of the two Sirens:\na fair wind drove her.
Then all at once the wind fell still, and a calm came,\nbreathless: some power lulled the waves to sleep.
My companions rose and furled the sails and stowed\nthem in the hollow ship, and sitting to the oars
they whitened the water with the polished blades of fir.
And I with my sharp bronze cut a great round cake of wax
into little pieces, and kneaded them in my heavy hands;
and quickly the wax grew warm,\nfor my great strength pressed it,
and the beam of the lord Helios, Hyperion's son;\nand one by one I stopped the ears of all my companions.
And they bound me in the ship, hand and foot together,
upright in the mast-step, and made\nthe rope-ends fast to the mast itself;
and sitting down they struck the\ngray salt water with their oars.
But when we were as far off as a man's shout carries,
running swiftly, the sea-quick ship did not slip past them
unseen as she leapt near —\nand they raised their clear-toned song:
'Come here, come, much-praised Odysseus,\ngreat glory of the Achaeans:
bring your ship in, so you may hear the voice of us two.
For no man yet has rowed past this place in his black ship
before hearing the honey-voiced song from our lips —
no: he has his delight of it,\nand goes his way knowing more.
For we know all that in wide Troy the Argives and\nthe Trojans labored through by the gods' will;
and we know all that comes to\npass on the nourishing earth.'
So they sang, sending out their\nbeautiful voice; and my heart
longed to listen, and I ordered my companions to free me,
signaling with my brows; but they\nthrew themselves forward and rowed.
And at once Perimedes and Eurylochus rose and bound\nme with more bonds, and squeezed them tighter.
But when they had driven past them, and we could\nno longer hear the Sirens' voice, or their singing,
quickly my trusted companions took out the wax I had\nstopped their ears with, and loosed me from my bonds.
But when we had left the island behind, at once I\nsaw smoke, and a great wave, and heard a booming.
The men were terrified: the oars flew from their hands
and clattered, all of them,\nalong the current; and the ship stopped
dead, since their hands no\nlonger drove the tapered blades.
And I went through the ship, heartening my companions\nwith gentle words, standing by each man in turn:
'Friends — we are not unschooled in evils, not we.
This evil that stands over us now\nis no greater than when the Cyclops
penned us in his hollow cave by brute force — and even\nfrom there, by my prowess and my counsel and my mind,
we escaped. Someday, I think,\nwe will remember this one too.
Come then — all of us — do exactly as I say.
You, keep to your benches and strike the deep surf
of the salt sea with your oar-blades, in hope Zeus\nsomehow may grant us to slip clear of this destruction;
and you, steersman, here is my order — lay it up
in your heart, since you handle the\nsteering-oar of our hollow ship:
keep the ship outside that smoke and that surf,\nand hug the crag, for fear the ship, before you know it,
shears off toward the other side —\nand you pitch us into the evil.'
So I spoke, and they quickly heeded my words.
But Scylla I did not speak of — that hopeless horror —\nfor fear my companions, terrified, might drop
the oars and pack themselves into the hold.
And then — Circe's hard command, that I should\nnot arm myself — I let it slip from my mind:
I put on my famous armor, took two long spears in\nmy hands, and went up to the half-deck at the bow,
for it was from there I expected the first sight of\nScylla of the rock, bringing ruin on my companions.
And I could not glimpse her anywhere; my eyes grew\nweary scanning every hand-span of the misty rock.
So we sailed up the narrows, wailing:
on this side Scylla; on that, shining Charybdis\ngulped down, terribly, the salt water of the sea.
When she vomited it up, like a cauldron over a great fire
she would seethe and boil in all\nher churning depth, and the spray
fell high on the very tops of both the crags;\nbut when she gulped the salt sea down again,
all her churning depth showed open,\nand the rock around her
roared terribly, and at the bottom the earth showed,\ndark-blue with sand. And the pale terror took them.
We looked to her, then, in our dread of destruction —\nand that was when Scylla snatched from the hollow ship
six of my companions, the best in hands and strength.
Turning to look at the fast ship, after my men,\nI caught their feet and hands already above me,
swung high aloft; and they cried out and called to me
by name — for the last time —\nin the anguish of their hearts.
As when a fisherman on a jutting rock, with his long rod,\ncasts down baits as a snare for the little fishes,
dropping into the sea the horn of a field-ox,\nand each fish he catches he flings up gasping onto the land:
so they were swung gasping up toward the rocks.
And there in her doorway she devoured them,\nshrieking as they were,
stretching their hands toward me in the terrible struggle.
That was the most pitiful thing my eyes ever looked on
of all I suffered searching out the pathways of the sea.
Now when we had escaped the rocks, and dread Charybdis\nand Scylla, we came quickly then to the god's
blameless island: there were the beautiful broad-browed
cattle, and the many strong flocks, of Helios Hyperion.
And while I was still at sea, in the black ship,\nI heard the lowing of cattle being folded
and the bleating of sheep; and there fell upon my\nheart the word of the blind seer, Theban Tiresias,
and of Circe of Aeaea, who charged me over and over\nto shun the island of Helios, the delight of mortals.
Then, grieving at heart, I spoke among my companions:
'Hear my words, companions, for all your suffering,\nso I may tell you the prophecies of Tiresias
and of Circe of Aeaea, who charged me over and over\nto shun the island of Helios, the delight of mortals:
there, she said, is the most terrible evil waiting for us.
No — drive the black ship on, wide of the island.'
So I spoke, and their own hearts broke within them.
And at once Eurylochus answered me — with a hateful word:
'You are a hard one, Odysseus.\nYour strength is beyond us; your limbs
never tire. Truly you are made\nof iron through and through —
you who will not let your companions, worn down with labor
and sleeplessness, set foot on land, where on this
sea-ringed island we might at\nlast make ready a savory supper;
no — just as we are, through the\nfast-falling night, you order us
to wander, driven off the island, over the misted sea.
Out of the nights are born the hard winds, the wreckers\nof ships. How would a man escape sheer destruction
if somehow, suddenly, a squall of wind should come,
South Wind or hard-blowing West,\nwhich more than any others
smash ships to pieces — in despite of the gods our lords?
No: for now let us yield to black night and\nmake our supper ready, staying by the fast ship;
at dawn we will board, and stand out onto the wide sea.'
So spoke Eurylochus, and the other companions approved.
And then I knew it: some power was plotting evils —\nand lifting my voice I spoke winged words to him:
'Eurylochus, you force my hand: I am one man alone.
But come — every one of you swear me a strong oath:
if we find some herd of cattle or great flock\nof sheep, let no man in his evil recklessness
kill one cow, one sheep. No: sit quiet\nand eat the food immortal Circe gave.'
So I spoke, and they swore at once, as I demanded.
And when they had sworn, and made an end of the oath,\nwe moored the well-made ship in the hollow harbor
close by a spring of sweet water, and the companions\nwent ashore, and skillfully made their supper ready.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,
they fell to weeping, remembering their dear companions
whom Scylla had snatched from the hollow ship and eaten;\nand as they wept, a deep sleep came upon them.
But in the night's third watch,\nwhen the stars had crossed their height,
Zeus who gathers the clouds\nroused a raging wind against us
in a howling squall, and covered land and sea\nalike with cloud; and night rose up out of heaven.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
we dragged the ship up and made her fast in a hollow cave
where the nymphs had their fine dancing-floors and seats;\nand then I called them all together, and said:
'Friends — there is food and drink in the fast ship:
let us keep our hands off these cattle,\nor we shall suffer for it.
These are the cattle and the\nstrong flocks of a terrible god —
Helios, who sees all things and hears all things.'
So I spoke, and their proud hearts consented.
Then for a whole month the South\nWind blew without let, and no other
wind rose after that, except the East and the South.
As long as the men had bread and red wine,\nthey kept their hands from the cattle:
But when all the ship's provisions were spent,\nand need drove them roaming after game —
fish, birds, whatever came to their dear hands —\nwith bent hooks, while hunger wore their bellies down,
then I went away up the island, to pray to the gods,\nin hope one might show me a road home.
And when, crossing the island,\nI had left my companions behind,
I washed my hands where there was shelter from the\nwind and prayed to all the gods who hold Olympus —
and they poured sweet sleep upon my eyelids.
And Eurylochus began his evil counsel to the companions:
'Hear my words, companions, for all your suffering.
All deaths are hateful to wretched mortals —
but to die of hunger, and meet\ndoom that way, is the most pitiful.
Come then: let us drive off the\nbest of the cattle of Helios
and sacrifice them to the immortals who hold wide heaven.
And if we come to Ithaca, our fathers' land,\nwe will build at once a rich temple to Helios Hyperion
and set up in it fine offerings, many of them.
But if, in anger over his straight-horned cattle, he wills
to destroy our ship, and the other gods go with him —\nI would rather gulp once at the wave and lose my life
than be starved slowly to death on a desert island.'
So spoke Eurylochus, and the other companions approved.
And at once they drove off the\nbest of the cattle of Helios,
from close by — for not far from the dark-blue-prowed ship
the beautiful broad-browed\ncrook-horned cattle were grazing —
and they stood around them and prayed to the gods,\nplucking the tender leaves of a high-crowned oak:
for they had no white barley aboard the well-benched ship.
And when they had prayed, and cut the throats, and flayed,
they carved out the thigh-pieces\nand wrapped them deep in fat,
folding it double, and laid raw flesh upon them;\nand they had no wine to pour over the blazing offerings,
so they made libation with water,\nand roasted all the entrails.
And when the thighs were burned through,\nand they had tasted the innards,
they carved up the rest and threaded it on spits.
Then it was that the deep sleep fled from my eyelids,
and I went down to the fast ship and the shore of the sea.
But as I came near the curved ship, the sweet\nsmell of the fat's smoke drifted all around me,
and I groaned aloud, and cried out to the deathless gods:
'Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever —
it was for my ruin, then, that you\nlaid me down in that pitiless sleep,
while my companions, waiting,\ndevised this monstrous thing.'
Swiftly the word came to Helios Hyperion:
long-robed Lampetie brought it —\nthat we had killed his cattle.
And at once, with anger in his heart,\nhe spoke among the immortals:
'Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever:
make them pay — the companions of Odysseus, Laertes' son —
who in their insolence have killed my cattle: the cattle
I took my joy in, every day I\nclimbed toward the starry heaven
and every day I turned from heaven back toward earth.
If they do not pay me a fitting price for the cattle,\nI will go down into Hades and shine among the dead.'
Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered him:
'Helios — you shine on among the immortals, surely,\nand among mortal men across the grain-giving plowland;
and as for those men: their fast ship I will soon strike
with the white lightning, and shatter it to\nsplinters in the middle of the wine-dark sea.'
— This I heard afterward from fair-haired Calypso;
and she said she heard it herself from Hermes the guide.\n— Now when I had come down to the ship and the sea,
I went up and down and rebuked them,\nman by man; but no remedy
could we find anywhere: the cattle were dead already.
And soon the gods began to show\nforth portents among the men:
the hides crawled; the meat on the spits was lowing,
the roasted and the raw; and there\nrose a sound as of cattle crying.
Six days after that my trusted companions
feasted on the cattle of Helios they\nhad driven off, the best of them;
but when Zeus the son of Cronos\nset the seventh day upon us,
then at last the wind fell from its raging squall,\nand we boarded at once and stood out onto the wide sea,
stepping the mast and hauling up the white sails.
But when we had left the island behind,\nand no other land showed anywhere — only sky and sea —
then the son of Cronos set a dark-blue cloud over\nthe hollow ship, and the deep went black beneath it.
And she ran on not much longer: for all at once came\nthe shrieking West Wind, raging in a great squall,
and the storm-blast snapped both forestays of the mast:
the mast toppled backward, and all its tackle spilled
down into the bilge; and in the stern of the ship the mast
struck the steersman's head, and crushed the bones of\nthe skull all together; and like a diver he dropped
from the half-deck, and his proud life left his bones.
And Zeus thundered in the same instant,\nand hurled his bolt into the ship,
and she shivered stem to stern,\nstruck by the bolt of Zeus,
and filled with the reek of sulfur;\nand the men fell from the ship.
Like sea-crows around the black hull
they were carried off on the waves;\nand the god took away their homecoming.
But I kept moving through the ship, until the surge
tore the sides loose from the keel,\nand the wave carried her stripped bare,
and snapped the mast off at the keel. But over the mast
the backstay had been flung — a thing made of ox-hide;\nwith it I lashed the two together, keel and mast,
and settling myself on them,\nI was carried before the deadly winds.
Then indeed the West Wind fell from its raging squall,
but the South came fast in its place,\nbringing anguish to my heart:
that I should measure back my way to deadly Charybdis.
All night I was carried; and with the rising sun\nI came to Scylla's crag, and to dread Charybdis.
She was gulping down the salt water of the sea —\nbut I, swinging up high toward the tall fig tree,
caught it and clung there like a bat. And there was no way
to plant my feet firm anywhere, no way to climb it:
the roots were far below, and the branches out of reach,\nlong and great boughs that shadowed Charybdis.
I clung there without slackening,\nuntil she should vomit back
the mast and keel again. And to my longing, late,
they came: at the hour when a man\nrises from the assembly for supper —
the judge of many quarrels among contending young men —
at that hour the timbers reappeared out of Charybdis.
I let go, feet and hands, from above, and dropped\nwith a crash into the water beyond the long timbers,
and settling on them, I rowed hard with my hands.
And Scylla — the father of men and gods did not let her
see me again: I would not have\nslipped clear of sheer destruction.
From there I was carried nine days;\nand on the tenth, in the black night,
the gods brought me near the island Ogygia, where Calypso
lives, she of the lovely braids,\nthe dread goddess with a mortal's voice,
and she loved me and cared for me.\nBut why tell that tale over?
Only yesterday I told it in this house —\nto you and to your strong wife. And it is hateful to me
to tell a tale over again that has been told out plainly."
